text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a warning about testosterone supplements in men. A
discovery in the lab which could increase the success rates of organ
transplantation. Should doctors be allowed to refuse care to patients because
they object to the treatment (the doctors that is) on moral or religious grounds? A
leading ethicist says no. And a paradox which emerged yesterday in an
Australian study published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine.

Obstructive sleep apnoea, usually where people snore badly and then stop
breathing for a few seconds at a time, is linked to a higher risk of heart disease,
so much so that some manufacturers of so-called CPAP machines where
positive air pressure through the nose keeps the airways open have suggested
that the machines reduced the chances of a heart attack or stroke. Now an
Australian trial suggests that isn't so. With me is one of the authors, sleep
specialist and researcher Professor Ron Grunstein. Welcome to the Health
Report.

Ron Grunstein: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: What is the link between sleep apnoea and heart disease?

Ron Grunstein: Look, I think there's quite strong and compelling evidence that
patients with sleep apnoea as a group have higher rates of cardiovascular
disease and cerebrovascular disease…

Norman Swan: Cerebrovascular meaning leading to stroke.

Ron Grunstein: Yes. So it's an association. But they also share a lot of the risk
factors that people who get those heart and brain disorders have, which is that
they are obese and they have some vascular risk factors. So the issue of
whether treatment of sleep apnoea could potentially reduce the risk of these
events happening in people has always been a challenge to the field.

Norman Swan: Which takes it from an association to cause and effect.

Ron Grunstein: Exactly.

Norman Swan: So rather than just be sitting side by side. Tell me what you did
in this trial?
 
Ron Grunstein: Well, the trial…when I think about it, it started about 11 years
ago, and it started really as a conversation by people who were in Australia who
were working in this field, we thought we needed to do this study. And my
colleague…

Norman Swan: And we have to say to begin with that the ancestors of your
group actually invented CPAP worldwide. The idea came from…

Ron Grunstein: Yes, it's an Australian invention. So my colleague Doug McAvoy
at Flinders University, and Craig Anderson at the George Institute in Sydney
really drove this study. And we set up an executive group to look at how to
design such a study. And basically we ended up recruiting about 2,700 or
randomising 2,700 patients into two groups, one who received this continuous
positive airway pressure, plus usual care, versus another group who were
randomised to usual care alone. Importantly the patients that we chose all had
pre-existing vascular events, they'd had a heart attack or they had angina with
proven cardiovascular disease.

Norman Swan: So they were at high risk of another…

Ron Grunstein: Yes, a high risk, because we were looking for higher return in
terms of event rates.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Ron Grunstein: Well, the primary finding was that after an average of 3.7 years
follow-up there was no difference in outcomes between the group that received
the CPAP therapy and usual care versus the usual care alone. So there was no
advantage of giving people CPAP if the aim of the exercise was to reduce
cardiovascular events and strokes. What we also found was there was a benefit
in reducing symptoms, sleepiness and impaired well-being, these got better. But
the primary endpoint, primary variable of interest was not achieved.

Norman Swan: What does that tell you about CPAP? Does this mean that
ResMed needs to put out a profit warning? We shouldn't pick out one in
particular. But essentially do the manufacturers have to change their marketing
now?
 
Ron Grunstein: Look, if you permit me to focus on what doctors should do…

Norman Swan: Okay, this is away from tiger country, all right!

Ron Grunstein: I think as people working in this area I think we really have to
interpret the evidence for our patients, which is that if…and I actually saw a
patient today who just happens to be a semi-retired cardiologist who has got very
few symptoms of sleep apnoea but he has got sleep apnoea and he has
previously had coronary bypass surgery…

Norman Swan: A cardiologist who walks the talk, clearly.

Ron Grunstein: Yes, and he kind of…so, what do I do for this gentleman? And
basically just purely on the basis of trying to improve his cardiovascular
prognosis, I don't think I've got the evidence from this study to justify that.
However, he may well have symptoms which may warrant treatment. So you
don't really want to treat this…you don't want to tell patients, look, I'm going to
give you this CPAP, even though you feel perfectly well, we are going to give you
a CPAP machine because it's going to reduce your future risk of recurrence of
heart disease or stroke.

Norman Swan: So it's just for the sleep apnoea itself. And just briefly in the
minute or two that we've got left, where does continuous positive airways
pressure sit amongst weight loss, surgical devices, things that you stick in your
mouth, splints and so on, in terms of benefits? We seem to be rolling the dice
totally on CPAP machines.

Ron Grunstein: To paraphrase one of our politicians, we live in exciting times.
The treatment choices are widening. We've studied extensively dental devices for
sleep apnoea which seem to work reasonably well when compared to CPAP.

Norman Swan: So these are like mouth guards?

Ron Grunstein: Yes, they are sort of splints that basically…you've got to make
them individually for the patient, and they essentially move the mandible, the
bottom jaw, forward, creating space behind the tongue. And these are
reasonably effective treatments when compared to CPAP.
 
Norman Swan: What about bariatric surgery? Does that relieve snoring and
sleep apnoea?

Ron Grunstein: Yes, I think bariatric surgery in people where there is other
health issues as well as sleep apnoea is probably justified. We've had quite good
success…because most of our patients are male, we've had very good success
with just diet, exercise and sustaining those effects for at least a year and getting
a reduction in sleep apnoea.

Norman Swan: Ron, thanks very much for joining us.

Ron Grunstein: No problem Norman.

Norman Swan: Ron Grunstein is chief investigator at the NHMRC Centre for
Translational Sleep and Circadian Neurobiology at the Wilcock Institute of
medical Research at the University of Sydney.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN, at ABC News Radio and CBC
radio in Canada, I'm Norman Swan, and we have links to the references for all
our stories, so if you want the references you can go to our website at ABC
Radio National.

Guidelines for doctors treating men with what's called hypogonadism have been
released by the Endocrine Society of Australia in today's edition of the Medical
Journal of Australia, and they contain a warning about the use of testosterone
supplements. One of the leaders of the group was Professor Bu Yeap of the
University of Western Australia School of Medicine and Pharmacology and he's
in our Perth studio. Welcome Bu to the Health Report.

Bu Yeap: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Just tell us what hypogonadism is.

Bu Yeap: So hypogonadism is a medical condition where you have a problem
with the pituitary gland or the testes and you are unable to make enough
testosterone for yourself. So your testosterone levels are low and it's associated
with a range of symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: Such as?
 
Bu Yeap: You may feel you've lost…your libido is low, so you've lost interest in
sex or you may feel tired or lethargic. Some men may notice that they seem to be
gaining fat, losing a bit of muscle. So they may actually present with reduced
bone mass as another example.

Norman Swan: So a fracture.

Bu Yeap: Yes, so there are quite a few different symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: So this isn't the male menopause. The reason for the loss of
testosterone is something else.

Bu Yeap: Yes, so we're talking about men who have medical conditions affecting
the hypothalamus or the pituitary gland or the testes who cannot make enough
testosterone for themselves.

Norman Swan: And just to explain, the testes, just like the ovaries, are driven by
the brain, hormones from the brain that send signals to the testes to produce
testosterone. So somewhere along that pathway things can go wrong.

Bu Yeap: Yes.

Norman Swan: And you told us how you have it. And is testosterone the only
treatment?

Bu Yeap: Well, there are two separate components. So obviously one function of
the testes is to make testosterone, the other one is to make sperm. So if you
want fertility and you have this kind of problem then it's a very different approach.
So if you actually want fertility then testosterone is actually…it may make things a
bit worse, so you have to sort that out first and then testosterone will treat
symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: So this can turn up in an IVF clinics with a couple who are
infertile and it turns out that it's the man's issue and it could be hypogonadism,
and then you've got to work out how you're going to treat it.

Bu Yeap: Yes, that's one of the possible ways it could present, yes.
 
Norman Swan: And for other men where infertility is not the issue, then what you
are doing is testosterone replacement.

Bu Yeap: Yes. And testosterone is the best hormone and there are different
formulations, so we can actually individualise treatment and find a formulation
that suits a particular man.

Norman Swan: What do you mean by different formulations?

Bu Yeap: You can give testosterone as an intramuscular injection or you can
give it as a gel or a cream or a liquid, so transdermally. So there are different
options and it depends upon the particular man's preference.

Norman Swan: And before we get onto just your recommendations, there is one
more thing I just wanted to ask you which is how you make the diagnosis of
hypogonadism apart from the story, because you don't want to say this is just
hypogonadism without knowing for sure.

Bu Yeap: The symptoms and signs are really important. The examination may
be quite helpful, and then obviously you do a blood test and you can measure
testosterone in the blood as well.

Norman Swan: And the hormones from the brain as well? Do they go up?

Bu Yeap: Yes, so we measure luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating
hormone, LH and FSH, and if you have a testicular problem they go up, whereas
if you have a problem in the pituitary gland they tend to be lower than normal.

Norman Swan: So there is ways of diagnosing this.

Bu Yeap: Yes.

Norman Swan: What's the issue with prescribing testosterone that you were
warning about in this guideline in today's Medical Journal of Australia?

Bu Yeap: The guidelines…the most important point is that we have
recommended that testosterone be given to men who have pathological
hypogonadism, they have a problem in the pituitary or in the testes. There are a
lot of other conditions where your testosterone may be low, and this includes
 
men who are older or men who have medical problems or men who may be
taking medications such as glucocorticoids or opioids.

Norman Swan: So steroids or morphine-like drugs.

Bu Yeap: So in those men, testosterone levels may be low, but we don't have
enough evidence to justify giving them testosterone, or at least not as yet.

Norman Swan: Right. Now, you're worried about heart disease.

Bu Yeap: Yes, there is a risk of adverse events, cardiovascular adverse events
and it seems to be in that those men who are older or frail and have already got
heart disease.

Norman Swan: You mean cardiovascular events…that's what I was talking to
Ron Grunstein a moment ago about, heart attacks, strokes, angina.

Bu Yeap: Yes, heart attacks and strokes, yes. So it might be that older men, frail
men and men who have already got cardiovascular disease, that we might just
have to be a little bit cautious in those men.

Norman Swan: What does that mean for a general practitioner or a specialist in
this area?

Bu Yeap: So if those men have pathological hypogonadism, they should still be
considered for treatment but you might want to initiate treatment little bit more
slowly or start at a lower dose and monitor more carefully. Obviously first you
what to make sure that whatever the existing heart disease is that it's under
treatment. For men who do not have pathological hypogonadism, well, we would
probably advise against giving them testosterone, particularly in the setting
where they may be at higher risk of adverse events…

Norman Swan: So if a man is feeling fatigued and claims that he is suffering
from the male menopause…

Bu Yeap: Okay, well, we don't like that term 'male menopause'…

Norman Swan: I was wondering how long it would take you to rise to the bait!
 
Bu Yeap: There is an important caveat in all of this which is that for the men
without pathological hypogonadism, there are a lot of areas where we
recommend that they shouldn't have testosterone, but because there's not
enough evidence this is an important area where we do need to do a lot more
research. Testosterone may have benefits, it may have risks, but we need to do
more research to clarify those.

Norman Swan: But coming to the bottom-line here, male hypogonadism is really
just about the only indication for testosterone at the moment on an evidence
base.

Bu Yeap: Yes, if you look at the evidence, if you have male hypogonadism then
yes, you should be treated. So yes, you could say that that's the case. And in all
the other scenarios that we've mentioned we really need to do more research to
define what the benefits and the risks are.

Norman Swan: And is there any such thing as the andropause?

Bu Yeap: The decline in testosterone as men grow older is actually very gradual.
So if you look at all the studies, our own included, older men, even if they are
very healthy will have lower testosterone than younger men, but there isn't the
abrupt decline that you see in women who go through the menopausal transition.

Norman Swan: But I thought your longitudinal study in Western Australia
showed that you had 80-year-old men with the testosterones of younger men
because they were very fit, they had good musculature and that in fact it's not an
inevitable part of ageing, that you've got this group of men who were pretty
testosterone loaded.

Bu Yeap: There are two studies, the one that you refer to is a slightly different
one from the one that we have done in Western Australia. You can have older
men who are really healthy and they have testosterone levels comparable to
younger men. But in our study, if you take a large group of really healthy 70- to
89-year-old men, then their testosterone levels, the range that you see is in fact
lower than healthy 21- to 35-year-olds.

Norman Swan: So there's the odd exception but the average bears out.
 
Bu Yeap: Well, this is an area which is…you could say there is ongoing debate
over this area. But yes, the reference range is low in really healthy older men, but
you can have very healthy older men with levels comparable to younger men.

Norman Swan: Bu Yeap, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Bu Yeap: Not at all, a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Professor Bu Yeap from the University of Western Australia's
School of Medicine and Pharmacology. And again, we'll have the references for
that story if you are concerned about hypogonadism on the Health Report's
website.

Researchers in Melbourne may have found a substance which helps to protect
organs such as kidneys being donated for transplantation from a common cause
of damage. If it pans out the result will be higher success rates from these
precious donations. The substance is called follistatin, and one of the research
leaders was Professor David de Kretser of the Hudson Institute of Medical
Research at Monash University, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome to
the Health Report David.

David de Krester: Nice to be here.

Norman Swan: What is the problem you are trying to solve here?

David de Krester: Well, basically transplants, when you take an organ out in,
say, Sydney, and the donor's match for him is in Melbourne, that transplant is off
its blood supply for maybe six, 10 hours, and when you get reperfusion of blood
you actually create an inflammatory response. And the inflammatory response
produces a substance called activin which is actually a hormonal stimulation but
is also the major controller of your body's inflammatory response. And so
theoretically…

Norman Swan: So this is called a reperfusion injury.

David de Krester: Yes, reperfusion injury is absolutely right, yes. And so
basically some studies that we've done shows that if you put actually follistatin
into the preservation solutions of organs, that you can actually attenuate that
damage and result in a better transplant. And especially in lung transplants
 
where you can get preservation of aeration, of the air sacs, but those air sacs
may not be supplied with blood, therefore it's sort of dead space essentially.

Norman Swan: I know the St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney has got this
innovation called 'heart in a box' where they perfuse hearts and manage to get
much greater success rates in terms of length of time. Is this a sort of technology
that you could add to to improve things?

David de Krester: Absolutely…

Norman Swan: And is it all organs? Because you did this study in kidneys.

David de Krester: We haven't done the studies in kidneys, we've done some
different studies in kidneys in that, again, basically if you interrupt the blood
supply to the kidneys for a period of time, you actually create an inflammatory
response, activin levels rise, and again, if you give the mouse follistatin before
you actually clamp the blood vessel to the kidney, you can actually attenuate and
decrease the damage. So follistatin is a very powerful substance which has the
potential for multiple applications associated with inflammation and tissue
damage.

Norman Swan: So the study that we've picked up on here is actually the study of
mice where you've shown that it works on this substance called activin to reduce
the injury in kidneys in mice. But if you were actually inhibiting inflammation, you
are messing with the immune system, could you get adverse immune effects by
this?

David de Krester: Look, that's one of the issues that also needs to be looked at
more closely. In an acute situation basically blocking the inflammatory response
is beneficial and there's data in wounding studies to show that if you give
follistatin you can actually decrease the degree of scar formation. So there are
multiple uses of this substance, and it is going to be a very powerful modulator of
inflammation.

Norman Swan: What happens in mice does not necessarily happen in humans.
What evidence have you got that this could work in human tissue?
 
David de Krester: Well, certainly the studies that I was describing in relationship
to transplantation and the rise in activin, those were done basically in blood
samples from patients who were undergoing human lung transplantations. So
this is showing that, if you like, the activin levels rise in relationship to certain
aspects of transplantation surgery, especially the ischemia. Also substances like
heparin, also anticoagulants, can release activin from tissue stores.

Norman Swan: So it could make it worse?

David de Krester: Activin is bound to follistatin through a positive charge
system, and heparin being negatively charged releases it. So if I was to give you
a single shot of heparin you would get a single pulse of activin and follistatin
released. If I gave you a squarewave you would get a squarewave. So basically
your tissues and surfaces of cells actually have a coating in their basement
membranes of activin and follistatin there.

Norman Swan: So you are trying to commercialise this. How long before you
think that you are able to do proper trials in humans and give it a go?

David de Krester: Well, we are now in a position…we've obviously gone from a
test tube to 1,000 litre fermentation to produce follistatin for human use. It has
been tested in two animal species without any side effects. It has been given
initially to humans in the first instance. And here again, one of the things that we
have to do in trials is to show that the drug is actually effective. Well, a normal
subject is actually not inflamed, so one actually has to create an inflammation in
a normal subject, and we are delivering follistatin for lung purposes using a
nebuliser system. So basically there was no experience here in Australia doing
that. We were able to do such a study in Manchester where there has been
previous studies like this done and showed very clearly that giving follistatin in a
nebuliser system actually decreased the number of white blood cells that are in
the sputum of men who have been exposed to lipopolysaccharide. So we've
proved efficacy in normal subjects.

Norman Swan: So you're on the runway. That is fascinating, thank you very
much for joining us on the Health Report.

David de Krester: It's a pleasure.
 
Norman Swan: Professor David de Krester of the Hudson Institute of Medical
Research at Monash University in Melbourne.

A leading ethicist is going to argue in a lecture in Queensland later this week that
doctors and other health professionals like pharmacists should not be allowed to
deny patients access to care because they, the doctors or pharmacists,
conscientiously object to it. The commonest examples would be contraception
and termination of pregnancy but there are others.

Professor Julian Savulescu joins me from our Brisbane studio. Julian is Professor
of Practical Ethics at the University of Oxford. Welcome to the Health Report,
Julian.

Julian Savulescu: Good evening.

Norman Swan: Just give me your argument. Roll it out.

Julian Savulescu: Well, there are two main arguments. By allowing a
conscientious objection clause, as Victorian legislation does, you open the door
to women being denied medical services. So one study in the United States
around 10 years ago reported 15% of doctors wouldn't inform people of
procedures that were legal, and 30% wouldn't refer on to another practitioner.
That means in the US about 100 million people are going to be denied some
medical service they are entitled to.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Julian Savulescu: Well, such as contraception, abortion, sterilisation, and in
those states where assisted suicide is legal, assisted suicide. The second main
argument is really a moral one; why should the medical care that the patient gets
depend on the personal values, often the religious values of the doctor that they
happen to attend? There are principles of law and ethics that should govern how
treatments are delivered to patients, and doctors should certainly have their own
values, but at the end of the day the patient should be entitled to receive medical
care that is legal that is in their interests and that they want.

Norman Swan: And do we know the extent of the problem in Australia?

Julian Savulescu: Well, there is certainly evidence…
 
Norman Swan: With the problem being, if you are right, denial of access to care.

Julian Savulescu: Well, if you are in a country town where the only general
practitioner has a religious objection to contraception or abortion, you're going to
be in trouble. And often this causes delays, so that what would have been early
terminations of pregnancy become late terminations of pregnancy, where the
fetus is then viable. So particularly in large countries such as Canada and
Australia, this has real implications for people that live in remote areas that are
effectively denied care. In some states of the United States there is only one
abortion clinic for a whole state because of this kind of phenomenon.

Norman Swan: Well, that's not necessarily the conscientious objection, that's
more the political environment of the States, isn't it?

Julian Savulescu: Well, it's people determining care on the basis of values
rather than on some legal and ethical principles, and I think you're going to see
effectively the same sorts of things in remote areas of Australia.

Norman Swan: So does that mean that when you are doing an interview for a
medical school, if you are a member of Opus Dei you don't get in or what?

Julian Savulescu: Well, in my view there is three ways to deal with it. One is
simply to not allow a legal right of conscientious objection, and that's precisely
what Sweden and Finland have done and they have excellent care for women
and they haven't discouraged good people from taking up medicine, and the
other one is to screen people on entry to medical school.

Norman Swan: So just give me that screening story again, because surely you
are not going to deny Catholics entry into…you know, highly religious believing
Catholics to medical school?

Julian Savulescu: There's plenty of specialities in medicine that you can do that
don't involve contraception, abortion or sterilisation. So what I don't understand is
if we say that, for example, sterilisation and contraception are a part of obstetrics
and gynaecology, why you would decide to enter that speciality if it was a
requirement of the job to deliver those services, that you could enter cardiology
or pathology or another specialty. So I think it's really a more efficient way of
organising a health system to make clear at the outset we expect doctors to be
 
providing these services in these specialities, and if you don't want to do that, do
another specialty.

Norman Swan: Can you really legislate for it, because we are quite happy about
conscientious objection when doctors don't participate in torture, for example,
and where they don't administer lethal injections in jurisdictions which have
capital punishment. So we are pretty happy with conscientious objection there.
Why are we getting antsy about termination and contraception?

Julian Savulescu: Well, torture is illegal and it's not desired by the patient and
it's not in the patient's interest, nor is capital punishment. Those procedures are
not part of medical practice that is governed by law and medical ethics. The point
that I'm making is that we want to have principles that will decide what is
appropriate within medicine, and clearly capital punishment and torture are not
appropriate medical practices. But when it comes to…we have a vote, we vote in
favour of euthanasia or abortion or contraception, then at one level the debate is
over. Doctors can still campaign for law reform. There are many practices in
medicine that are a part of medical practices that I think are immoral and result in
people's deaths, such as refusing to take organs from people who have signed
organ donation cards, I think that is immoral and it results in people's death. But if
in the end people are allowed to or families are allowed to prevent that, we have
to respect that and try to change things by engaging in political or moral debate.

Norman Swan: So you are suggesting legislation?

Julian Savulescu: As Sweden and Finland have shown, you can remove a legal
right of conscientious objection and deal with these issues as you deal with all
labour law where there is negotiations between individual doctors and their
employer around their own personal values. If there are a small number of
doctors who happen to be objecting to a particular practice and many other
doctors who can fulfil that need, that can be accommodated. But what you rapidly
see where it becomes a right is many people exercise that right, and often
because it's easier for them not to be involved in the performance of those sorts
of procedures. And I think at the end of the day it's the patient that suffers in
favour of the doctor's clean conscience.
 
Norman Swan: Given that that getting legislation like this through in the
Australian environment is unlikely, what would be the role of medical boards in
this, do you believe?

Julian Savulescu: I think medical boards and indeed medical schools should be
encouraging doctors to take a 21st century view of the doctor–patient relationship
where the patient is first and their own personal values are second. They can
engage in discussion with the patient about the options and perhaps even their
moral validity, but in the end they ought to be there serving the patient and
providing a service. So if indeed we have a right of conscientious objection, we
ought to be encouraging doctors only to exercise that right in the most extreme of
circumstances.

Norman Swan: Julian, thanks for joining us.

Julian Savulescu: My pleasure.

Norman Swan: Julian Savulescu, who is Professor of Practical Ethics at the
University of Oxford.

I'm Norman Swan and you've been listening to the Health Report here on RN,
ABC News Radio and CBC radio in Canada. Look forward to your company next
week.

Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a warning about testosterone supplements in men. A
discovery in the lab which could increase the success rates of organ
transplantation. Should doctors be allowed to refuse care to patients because
they object to the treatment (the doctors that is) on moral or religious grounds? A
leading ethicist says no. And a paradox which emerged yesterday in an
Australian study published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine.

Obstructive sleep apnoea, usually where people snore badly and then stop
breathing for a few seconds at a time, is linked to a higher risk of heart disease,
so much so that some manufacturers of so-called CPAP machines where
positive air pressure through the nose keeps the airways open have suggested
that the machines reduced the chances of a heart attack or stroke. Now an
Australian trial suggests that isn't so. With me is one of the authors, sleep
specialist and researcher Professor Ron Grunstein. Welcome to the Health
Report.

Ron Grunstein: Good evening Norman.

Norman Swan: What is the link between sleep apnoea and heart disease?

Ron Grunstein: Look, I think there's quite strong and compelling evidence that
patients with sleep apnoea as a group have higher rates of cardiovascular
disease and cerebrovascular disease…

Norman Swan: Cerebrovascular meaning leading to stroke.

Ron Grunstein: Yes. So it's an association. But they also share a lot of the risk
factors that people who get those heart and brain disorders have, which is that
they are obese and they have some vascular risk factors. So the issue of
whether treatment of sleep apnoea could potentially reduce the risk of these
events happening in people has always been a challenge to the field.

Norman Swan: Which takes it from an association to cause and effect.

Ron Grunstein: Exactly.

Norman Swan: So rather than just be sitting side by side. Tell me what you did
in this trial?

Ron Grunstein: Well, the trial…when I think about it, it started about 11 years
ago, and it started really as a conversation by people who were in Australia who
were working in this field, we thought we needed to do this study. And my
colleague…

Norman Swan: And we have to say to begin with that the ancestors of your
group actually invented CPAP worldwide. The idea came from…

Ron Grunstein: Yes, it's an Australian invention. So my colleague Doug McAvoy
at Flinders University, and Craig Anderson at the George Institute in Sydney
really drove this study. And we set up an executive group to look at how to
design such a study. And basically we ended up recruiting about 2,700 or
randomising 2,700 patients into two groups, one who received this continuous
positive airway pressure, plus usual care, versus another group who were
randomised to usual care alone. Importantly the patients that we chose all had
pre-existing vascular events, they'd had a heart attack or they had angina with
proven cardiovascular disease.

Norman Swan: So they were at high risk of another…

Ron Grunstein: Yes, a high risk, because we were looking for higher return in
terms of event rates.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Ron Grunstein: Well, the primary finding was that after an average of 3.7 years
follow-up there was no difference in outcomes between the group that received
the CPAP therapy and usual care versus the usual care alone. So there was no
advantage of giving people CPAP if the aim of the exercise was to reduce
cardiovascular events and strokes. What we also found was there was a benefit
in reducing symptoms, sleepiness and impaired well-being, these got better. But
the primary endpoint, primary variable of interest was not achieved.

Norman Swan: What does that tell you about CPAP? Does this mean that
ResMed needs to put out a profit warning? We shouldn't pick out one in
particular. But essentially do the manufacturers have to change their marketing
now?

Ron Grunstein: Look, if you permit me to focus on what doctors should do…

Norman Swan: Okay, this is away from tiger country, all right!

Ron Grunstein: I think as people working in this area I think we really have to
interpret the evidence for our patients, which is that if…and I actually saw a
patient today who just happens to be a semi-retired cardiologist who has got very
few symptoms of sleep apnoea but he has got sleep apnoea and he has
previously had coronary bypass surgery…

Norman Swan: A cardiologist who walks the talk, clearly.

Ron Grunstein: Yes, and he kind of…so, what do I do for this gentleman? And
basically just purely on the basis of trying to improve his cardiovascular
prognosis, I don't think I've got the evidence from this study to justify that.
However, he may well have symptoms which may warrant treatment. So you
don't really want to treat this…you don't want to tell patients, look, I'm going to
give you this CPAP, even though you feel perfectly well, we are going to give you
a CPAP machine because it's going to reduce your future risk of recurrence of
heart disease or stroke.

Norman Swan: So it's just for the sleep apnoea itself. And just briefly in the
minute or two that we've got left, where does continuous positive airways
pressure sit amongst weight loss, surgical devices, things that you stick in your
mouth, splints and so on, in terms of benefits? We seem to be rolling the dice
totally on CPAP machines.

Ron Grunstein: To paraphrase one of our politicians, we live in exciting times.
The treatment choices are widening. We've studied extensively dental devices for
sleep apnoea which seem to work reasonably well when compared to CPAP.

Norman Swan: So these are like mouth guards?

Ron Grunstein: Yes, they are sort of splints that basically…you've got to make
them individually for the patient, and they essentially move the mandible, the
bottom jaw, forward, creating space behind the tongue. And these are
reasonably effective treatments when compared to CPAP.

Norman Swan: What about bariatric surgery? Does that relieve snoring and
sleep apnoea?

Ron Grunstein: Yes, I think bariatric surgery in people where there is other
health issues as well as sleep apnoea is probably justified. We've had quite good
success…because most of our patients are male, we've had very good success
with just diet, exercise and sustaining those effects for at least a year and getting
a reduction in sleep apnoea.

Norman Swan: Ron, thanks very much for joining us.

Ron Grunstein: No problem Norman.

Norman Swan: Ron Grunstein is chief investigator at the NHMRC Centre for
Translational Sleep and Circadian Neurobiology at the Wilcock Institute of
medical Research at the University of Sydney.

Guidelines for doctors treating men with what's called hypogonadism have been
released by the Endocrine Society of Australia in today's edition of the Medical
Journal of Australia, and they contain a warning about the use of testosterone
supplements. One of the leaders of the group was Professor Bu Yeap of the
University of Western Australia School of Medicine and Pharmacology and he's
in our Perth studio. Welcome Bu to the Health Report.

Bu Yeap: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Just tell us what hypogonadism is.

Bu Yeap: So hypogonadism is a medical condition where you have a problem
with the pituitary gland or the testes and you are unable to make enough
testosterone for yourself. So your testosterone levels are low and it's associated
with a range of symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Bu Yeap: You may feel you've lost…your libido is low, so you've lost interest in
sex or you may feel tired or lethargic. Some men may notice that they seem to be
gaining fat, losing a bit of muscle. So they may actually present with reduced
bone mass as another example.

Norman Swan: So a fracture.

Bu Yeap: Yes, so there are quite a few different symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: So this isn't the male menopause. The reason for the loss of
testosterone is something else.

Bu Yeap: Yes, so we're talking about men who have medical conditions affecting
the hypothalamus or the pituitary gland or the testes who cannot make enough
testosterone for themselves.

Norman Swan: And just to explain, the testes, just like the ovaries, are driven by
the brain, hormones from the brain that send signals to the testes to produce
testosterone. So somewhere along that pathway things can go wrong.

Bu Yeap: Yes.

Norman Swan: And you told us how you have it. And is testosterone the only
treatment?

Bu Yeap: Well, there are two separate components. So obviously one function of
the testes is to make testosterone, the other one is to make sperm. So if you
want fertility and you have this kind of problem then it's a very different approach.
So if you actually want fertility then testosterone is actually…it may make things a
bit worse, so you have to sort that out first and then testosterone will treat
symptoms and signs.

Norman Swan: So this can turn up in an IVF clinics with a couple who are
infertile and it turns out that it's the man's issue and it could be hypogonadism,
and then you've got to work out how you're going to treat it.

Bu Yeap: Yes, that's one of the possible ways it could present, yes.

Norman Swan: And for other men where infertility is not the issue, then what you
are doing is testosterone replacement.

Bu Yeap: Yes. And testosterone is the best hormone and there are different
formulations, so we can actually individualise treatment and find a formulation
that suits a particular man.

Norman Swan: What do you mean by different formulations?

Bu Yeap: You can give testosterone as an intramuscular injection or you can
give it as a gel or a cream or a liquid, so transdermally. So there are different
options and it depends upon the particular man's preference.

Norman Swan: And before we get onto just your recommendations, there is one
more thing I just wanted to ask you which is how you make the diagnosis of
hypogonadism apart from the story, because you don't want to say this is just
hypogonadism without knowing for sure.

Bu Yeap: The symptoms and signs are really important. The examination may
be quite helpful, and then obviously you do a blood test and you can measure
testosterone in the blood as well.

Norman Swan: And the hormones from the brain as well? Do they go up?

Bu Yeap: Yes, so we measure luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating
hormone, LH and FSH, and if you have a testicular problem they go up, whereas
if you have a problem in the pituitary gland they tend to be lower than normal.

Norman Swan: So there is ways of diagnosing this.

Bu Yeap: Yes.

Norman Swan: What's the issue with prescribing testosterone that you were
warning about in this guideline in today's Medical Journal of Australia?

Bu Yeap: The guidelines…the most important point is that we have
recommended that testosterone be given to men who have pathological
hypogonadism, they have a problem in the pituitary or in the testes. There are a
lot of other conditions where your testosterone may be low, and this includes

men who are older or men who have medical problems or men who may be
taking medications such as glucocorticoids or opioids.

Norman Swan: So steroids or morphine-like drugs.

Bu Yeap: So in those men, testosterone levels may be low, but we don't have
enough evidence to justify giving them testosterone, or at least not as yet.

Norman Swan: Right. Now, you're worried about heart disease.

Bu Yeap: Yes, there is a risk of adverse events, cardiovascular adverse events
and it seems to be in that those men who are older or frail and have already got
heart disease.

Norman Swan: You mean cardiovascular events…that's what I was talking to
Ron Grunstein a moment ago about, heart attacks, strokes, angina.

Bu Yeap: Yes, heart attacks and strokes, yes. So it might be that older men, frail
men and men who have already got cardiovascular disease, that we might just
have to be a little bit cautious in those men.

Norman Swan: What does that mean for a general practitioner or a specialist in
this area?

Bu Yeap: So if those men have pathological hypogonadism, they should still be
considered for treatment but you might want to initiate treatment little bit more
slowly or start at a lower dose and monitor more carefully. Obviously first you
what to make sure that whatever the existing heart disease is that it's under
treatment. For men who do not have pathological hypogonadism, well, we would
probably advise against giving them testosterone, particularly in the setting
where they may be at higher risk of adverse events…

Norman Swan: So if a man is feeling fatigued and claims that he is suffering
from the male menopause…

Bu Yeap: Okay, well, we don't like that term 'male menopause'…

Norman Swan: I was wondering how long it would take you to rise to the bait!

Bu Yeap: There is an important caveat in all of this which is that for the men
without pathological hypogonadism, there are a lot of areas where we
recommend that they shouldn't have testosterone, but because there's not
enough evidence this is an important area where we do need to do a lot more
research. Testosterone may have benefits, it may have risks, but we need to do
more research to clarify those.

Norman Swan: But coming to the bottom-line here, male hypogonadism is really
just about the only indication for testosterone at the moment on an evidence
base.

Bu Yeap: Yes, if you look at the evidence, if you have male hypogonadism then
yes, you should be treated. So yes, you could say that that's the case. And in all
the other scenarios that we've mentioned we really need to do more research to
define what the benefits and the risks are.

Norman Swan: And is there any such thing as the andropause?

Bu Yeap: The decline in testosterone as men grow older is actually very gradual.
So if you look at all the studies, our own included, older men, even if they are
very healthy will have lower testosterone than younger men, but there isn't the
abrupt decline that you see in women who go through the menopausal transition.

Norman Swan: But I thought your longitudinal study in Western Australia
showed that you had 80-year-old men with the testosterones of younger men
because they were very fit, they had good musculature and that in fact it's not an
inevitable part of ageing, that you've got this group of men who were pretty
testosterone loaded.

Bu Yeap: There are two studies, the one that you refer to is a slightly different
one from the one that we have done in Western Australia. You can have older
men who are really healthy and they have testosterone levels comparable to
younger men. But in our study, if you take a large group of really healthy 70- to
89-year-old men, then their testosterone levels, the range that you see is in fact
lower than healthy 21- to 35-year-olds.

Norman Swan: So there's the odd exception but the average bears out.

Bu Yeap: Well, this is an area which is…you could say there is ongoing debate
over this area. But yes, the reference range is low in really healthy older men, but
you can have very healthy older men with levels comparable to younger men.

Norman Swan: Bu Yeap, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Bu Yeap: Not at all, a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Professor Bu Yeap from the University of Western Australia's
School of Medicine and Pharmacology. And again, we'll have the references for
that story if you are concerned about hypogonadism on the Health Report's
website.

Researchers in Melbourne may have found a substance which helps to protect
organs such as kidneys being donated for transplantation from a common cause
of damage. If it pans out the result will be higher success rates from these
precious donations. The substance is called follistatin, and one of the research
leaders was Professor David de Kretser of the Hudson Institute of Medical
Research at Monash University, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome to
the Health Report David.

David de Krester: Nice to be here.

Norman Swan: What is the problem you are trying to solve here?

David de Krester: Well, basically transplants, when you take an organ out in,
say, Sydney, and the donor's match for him is in Melbourne, that transplant is off
its blood supply for maybe six, 10 hours, and when you get reperfusion of blood
you actually create an inflammatory response. And the inflammatory response
produces a substance called activin which is actually a hormonal stimulation but
is also the major controller of your body's inflammatory response. And so
theoretically…

Norman Swan: So this is called a reperfusion injury.

David de Krester: Yes, reperfusion injury is absolutely right, yes. And so
basically some studies that we've done shows that if you put actually follistatin
into the preservation solutions of organs, that you can actually attenuate that
damage and result in a better transplant. And especially in lung transplants

where you can get preservation of aeration, of the air sacs, but those air sacs
may not be supplied with blood, therefore it's sort of dead space essentially.

Norman Swan: I know the St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney has got this
innovation called 'heart in a box' where they perfuse hearts and manage to get
much greater success rates in terms of length of time. Is this a sort of technology
that you could add to to improve things?

David de Krester: Absolutely…

Norman Swan: And is it all organs? Because you did this study in kidneys.

David de Krester: We haven't done the studies in kidneys, we've done some
different studies in kidneys in that, again, basically if you interrupt the blood
supply to the kidneys for a period of time, you actually create an inflammatory
response, activin levels rise, and again, if you give the mouse follistatin before
you actually clamp the blood vessel to the kidney, you can actually attenuate and
decrease the damage. So follistatin is a very powerful substance which has the
potential for multiple applications associated with inflammation and tissue
damage.

Norman Swan: So the study that we've picked up on here is actually the study of
mice where you've shown that it works on this substance called activin to reduce
the injury in kidneys in mice. But if you were actually inhibiting inflammation, you
are messing with the immune system, could you get adverse immune effects by
this?

David de Krester: Look, that's one of the issues that also needs to be looked at
more closely. In an acute situation basically blocking the inflammatory response
is beneficial and there's data in wounding studies to show that if you give
follistatin you can actually decrease the degree of scar formation. So there are
multiple uses of this substance, and it is going to be a very powerful modulator of
inflammation.

Norman Swan: What happens in mice does not necessarily happen in humans.
What evidence have you got that this could work in human tissue?

David de Krester: Well, certainly the studies that I was describing in relationship
to transplantation and the rise in activin, those were done basically in blood
samples from patients who were undergoing human lung transplantations. So
this is showing that, if you like, the activin levels rise in relationship to certain
aspects of transplantation surgery, especially the ischemia. Also substances like
heparin, also anticoagulants, can release activin from tissue stores.

Norman Swan: So it could make it worse?

David de Krester: Activin is bound to follistatin through a positive charge
system, and heparin being negatively charged releases it. So if I was to give you
a single shot of heparin you would get a single pulse of activin and follistatin
released. If I gave you a squarewave you would get a squarewave. So basically
your tissues and surfaces of cells actually have a coating in their basement
membranes of activin and follistatin there.

Norman Swan: So you are trying to commercialise this. How long before you
think that you are able to do proper trials in humans and give it a go?

David de Krester: Well, we are now in a position…we've obviously gone from a
test tube to 1,000 litre fermentation to produce follistatin for human use. It has
been tested in two animal species without any side effects. It has been given
initially to humans in the first instance. And here again, one of the things that we
have to do in trials is to show that the drug is actually effective. Well, a normal
subject is actually not inflamed, so one actually has to create an inflammation in
a normal subject, and we are delivering follistatin for lung purposes using a
nebuliser system. So basically there was no experience here in Australia doing
that. We were able to do such a study in Manchester where there has been
previous studies like this done and showed very clearly that giving follistatin in a
nebuliser system actually decreased the number of white blood cells that are in
the sputum of men who have been exposed to lipopolysaccharide. So we've
proved efficacy in normal subjects.

Norman Swan: So you're on the runway. That is fascinating, thank you very
much for joining us on the Health Report.

David de Krester: It's a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Professor David de Krester of the Hudson Institute of Medical
Research at Monash University in Melbourne.

A leading ethicist is going to argue in a lecture in Queensland later this week that
doctors and other health professionals like pharmacists should not be allowed to
deny patients access to care because they, the doctors or pharmacists,
conscientiously object to it. The commonest examples would be contraception
and termination of pregnancy but there are others.

Professor Julian Savulescu joins me from our Brisbane studio. Julian is Professor
of Practical Ethics at the University of Oxford. Welcome to the Health Report,
Julian.

Julian Savulescu: Good evening.

Norman Swan: Just give me your argument. Roll it out.

Julian Savulescu: Well, there are two main arguments. By allowing a
conscientious objection clause, as Victorian legislation does, you open the door
to women being denied medical services. So one study in the United States
around 10 years ago reported 15% of doctors wouldn't inform people of
procedures that were legal, and 30% wouldn't refer on to another practitioner.
That means in the US about 100 million people are going to be denied some
medical service they are entitled to.

Norman Swan: Such as?

Julian Savulescu: Well, such as contraception, abortion, sterilisation, and in
those states where assisted suicide is legal, assisted suicide. The second main
argument is really a moral one; why should the medical care that the patient gets
depend on the personal values, often the religious values of the doctor that they
happen to attend? There are principles of law and ethics that should govern how
treatments are delivered to patients, and doctors should certainly have their own
values, but at the end of the day the patient should be entitled to receive medical
care that is legal that is in their interests and that they want.

Norman Swan: And do we know the extent of the problem in Australia?

Julian Savulescu: Well, there is certainly evidence…

Norman Swan: With the problem being, if you are right, denial of access to care.

Julian Savulescu: Well, if you are in a country town where the only general
practitioner has a religious objection to contraception or abortion, you're going to
be in trouble. And often this causes delays, so that what would have been early
terminations of pregnancy become late terminations of pregnancy, where the
fetus is then viable. So particularly in large countries such as Canada and
Australia, this has real implications for people that live in remote areas that are
effectively denied care. In some states of the United States there is only one
abortion clinic for a whole state because of this kind of phenomenon.

Norman Swan: Well, that's not necessarily the conscientious objection, that's
more the political environment of the States, isn't it?

Julian Savulescu: Well, it's people determining care on the basis of values
rather than on some legal and ethical principles, and I think you're going to see
effectively the same sorts of things in remote areas of Australia.

Norman Swan: So does that mean that when you are doing an interview for a
medical school, if you are a member of Opus Dei you don't get in or what?

Julian Savulescu: Well, in my view there is three ways to deal with it. One is
simply to not allow a legal right of conscientious objection, and that's precisely
what Sweden and Finland have done and they have excellent care for women
and they haven't discouraged good people from taking up medicine, and the
other one is to screen people on entry to medical school.

Norman Swan: So just give me that screening story again, because surely you
are not going to deny Catholics entry into…you know, highly religious believing
Catholics to medical school?

Julian Savulescu: There's plenty of specialities in medicine that you can do that
don't involve contraception, abortion or sterilisation. So what I don't understand is
if we say that, for example, sterilisation and contraception are a part of obstetrics
and gynaecology, why you would decide to enter that speciality if it was a
requirement of the job to deliver those services, that you could enter cardiology
or pathology or another specialty. So I think it's really a more efficient way of
organising a health system to make clear at the outset we expect doctors to be

providing these services in these specialities, and if you don't want to do that, do
another specialty.

Norman Swan: Can you really legislate for it, because we are quite happy about
conscientious objection when doctors don't participate in torture, for example,
and where they don't administer lethal injections in jurisdictions which have
capital punishment. So we are pretty happy with conscientious objection there.
Why are we getting antsy about termination and contraception?

Julian Savulescu: Well, torture is illegal and it's not desired by the patient and
it's not in the patient's interest, nor is capital punishment. Those procedures are
not part of medical practice that is governed by law and medical ethics. The point
that I'm making is that we want to have principles that will decide what is
appropriate within medicine, and clearly capital punishment and torture are not
appropriate medical practices. But when it comes to…we have a vote, we vote in
favour of euthanasia or abortion or contraception, then at one level the debate is
over. Doctors can still campaign for law reform. There are many practices in
medicine that are a part of medical practices that I think are immoral and result in
people's deaths, such as refusing to take organs from people who have signed
organ donation cards, I think that is immoral and it results in people's death. But if
in the end people are allowed to or families are allowed to prevent that, we have
to respect that and try to change things by engaging in political or moral debate.

Norman Swan: So you are suggesting legislation?

Julian Savulescu: As Sweden and Finland have shown, you can remove a legal
right of conscientious objection and deal with these issues as you deal with all
labour law where there is negotiations between individual doctors and their
employer around their own personal values. If there are a small number of
doctors who happen to be objecting to a particular practice and many other
doctors who can fulfil that need, that can be accommodated. But what you rapidly
see where it becomes a right is many people exercise that right, and often
because it's easier for them not to be involved in the performance of those sorts
of procedures. And I think at the end of the day it's the patient that suffers in
favour of the doctor's clean conscience.

Norman Swan: Given that that getting legislation like this through in the
Australian environment is unlikely, what would be the role of medical boards in
this, do you believe?

Julian Savulescu: I think medical boards and indeed medical schools should be
encouraging doctors to take a 21st century view of the doctor–patient relationship
where the patient is first and their own personal values are second. They can
engage in discussion with the patient about the options and perhaps even their
moral validity, but in the end they ought to be there serving the patient and
providing a service. So if indeed we have a right of conscientious objection, we
ought to be encouraging doctors only to exercise that right in the most extreme of
circumstances.

Norman Swan: Julian, thanks for joining us.

Julian Savulescu: My pleasure.

Norman Swan: Julian Savulescu, who is Professor of Practical Ethics at the
University of Oxford.

I'm Norman Swan and you've been listening to the Health Report here on RN,
ABC News Radio and CBC radio in Canada. Look forward to your company next
week.
